sections.title: The Peace Offering
observations: Leviticus 3 introduces the concept of the peace offering, also known as the fellowship offering. This offering symbolizes the believer's desire for peace and fellowship with God, as well as with others.

The peace offering can be made from the herd or the flock, indicating that it is a voluntary act of worship rather than a mandatory sacrifice. This reflects the grace of God, who desires relationship over mere ritual.

The offerer lays their hands on the animal's head, signifying the transfer of their sin and guilt to the offering, which is then sacrificed. This act of laying on of hands is a powerful symbol of identification with the offering.

sections.title: The Role of the Priest
observations: The priest plays a crucial role in the peace offering, as they are responsible for presenting the offering before the Lord. This highlights the importance of the priestly mediation in the Old Testament sacrificial system.

The fat of the animal is to be burned on the altar, which is considered a pleasing aroma to the Lord. This signifies that the offering is accepted by God and that the worshiper is in right standing with Him.

sections.title: The Regulations for Offerings
observations: The chapter concludes with specific regulations regarding the types of animals that can be offered and the parts that are to be burned. These regulations emphasize the holiness of God and the seriousness of approaching Him in worship.

The distinction between clean and unclean animals is also significant, as it reflects God's desire for purity in worship. This serves as a reminder that our approach to God must be done with reverence and in accordance with His standards.

importantVerses.commentary: The fat of the peace offering is burned on the altar, symbolizing the worshiper's dedication and the acceptance of the offering by God.
The priest's role in the offering signifies the importance of mediation in approaching God, foreshadowing the ultimate priesthood of Christ.

questions: What does the peace offering teach us about our relationship with God and others?
How does the concept of mediation in the Old Testament sacrificial system point to the work of Christ?
In what ways can we apply the principles of the peace offering in our worship today?
